nameStory: Yellow onion gets its name from its bright golden-yellow star-shaped flowers that bloom in cheerful clusters. The scientific name 'moly' comes from ancient Greek mythology - it was the magical herb that Hermes gave to Odysseus to protect him from Circe's spells, though whether this little bulb is actually the legendary plant remains a delightful mystery.
description: Yellow onion is a charming bulbous perennial that escaped from gardens to occasionally naturalize in New England. This Mediterranean native produces clusters of bright yellow, star-shaped flowers atop slender stems in late spring to early summer. The plant grows 8-12 inches tall with narrow, gray-green leaves that emerge from an underground bulb, creating small colonies over time when happy in a location.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright golden-yellow flowers arranged in loose, flat-topped clusters of 5-20 blooms, each flower star-shaped with 6 pointed petals that feel papery when touched

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, strap-like gray-green leaves about 1/2 inch wide that feel smooth and slightly waxy, growing directly from the base with no stem leaves

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low-growing plant reaching 8-12 inches tall, often forming small patches as bulbs multiply underground over several seasons

idTips.label: Scent
idTips.description: Leaves and bulbs smell distinctly oniony when crushed or bruised, though milder and sweeter than common cooking onions

idTips.label: Bulbs
idTips.description: Small white bulbs about 1/2 inch across that feel firm and smooth, often producing smaller offset bulbs clustered around the main one

habitat: Yellow onion occasionally escapes cultivation to naturalize in sunny, well-drained locations like old garden sites, meadow edges, and disturbed areas with sandy or loamy soil. It prefers spots that get full sun to light shade and tolerates drought once established. Look for it near old homesites or areas where ornamental bulbs might have been planted and forgotten.

seasonality.spring: Gray-green leaves emerge in early spring, followed by flower buds on slender stalks. The distinctive onion scent is strongest when leaves are actively growing.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow star-shaped flowers bloom from late spring into early summer, creating showy golden clusters. Seeds develop in small capsules after flowering ends.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back as the plant enters dormancy. This is when bulbs can be divided if you find a patch.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground growth visible, existing only as bulbs underground until spring returns.

funFact: This little bulb is completely edible and was once considered so powerful that ancient Greeks believed it could counteract magic spells - Odysseus used it to resist the sorceress Circe's attempts to turn him into a pig!
confusionNotes: Yellow onion might be confused with wild garlic or other Allium species, but the bright golden-yellow flowers are distinctive - most wild onions have white, pink, or purple blooms. The oniony smell when crushed confirms it's in the onion family. Remember: golden flowers plus onion scent equals yellow onion.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'yellow onion,' this is not the same as the cooking onions you buy at the grocery store (Allium cepa). The common name can be confusing since we usually think of yellow onions as the big bulbs in our kitchen, but this ornamental species is much smaller and primarily grown for its flowers rather than culinary use.
compareHints: Yellow onion stands out from other New England Alliums by its bright golden-yellow flowers - most wild onions and garlics have white, pink, or purple blooms. Wild leek has broader leaves and white flowers, while wild garlic tends to have pinkish flowers and very narrow, almost grass-like leaves. The cheerful yellow flower clusters make this species unmistakable when in bloom.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wide leek stands out from other wild onions by having broad, flat leaves instead of narrow, tubular ones.
Wild garlic differs from other Alliums by its completely hollow, tubular leaves - wild leeks have flat, broad leaves, while chives have thin but solid leaves.
Unlike their larger cousins wild leek (ramps) which have broad, flat leaves, or wild garlic with its flat, grass-like foliage, chives have distinctively round, hollow leaves that are much thinner.

Among New England Alliums, garlic chives are unique for their flat, strap-like leaves - wild garlic has narrow tubular leaves, ramps have broad oval leaves, and regular chives have hollow cylindrical leaves.
Canadian Meadow Garlic differs from its cousin Wild Leek (ramps) by having thin, grass-like leaves rather than broad, flat leaves, and it grows in sunny areas rather than shaded forests.
Among New England's wild onions, nodding onion is the only one with distinctively drooping flower heads—wild garlic and field garlic hold their flowers upright in tight, rounded clusters.
Unlike other New England Alliums such as wild garlic, chives, or wild leeks that produce typical flower clusters, Egyptian Walking Onion is unmistakable with its bulblet clusters.
Among its Allium relatives, garlic is distinguished by its segmented bulb structure — wild onions and leeks have single, solid bulbs rather than the characteristic cloves.
Common onions differ from their wild Allium relatives by having distinctly hollow, tubular leaves and that familiar sharp kitchen-onion scent.
Ramsons stands out from other New England wild onions by having the broadest, flattest leaves in the genus - most other Alliums here have narrow, grass-like or tubular leaves.

Wild leek stands out from other New England Alliums by being much larger and more robust - while wild garlic and chives have thin, grass-like leaves, and ramps have broad leaves that disappear before flowering, wild leek maintains its broad, blue-green leaves right through the blooming period.
Field garlic differs from wild garlic by having flower heads that contain both actual flowers and bulblets mixed together, while wild garlic usually produces only bulblets.
Unlike New England's native wild onions such as wild leek or wild garlic which have narrow, grass-like green leaves, Turkistan onion stands out with its broad, silvery-blue foliage.

Small Yellow Onion stands out dramatically from other New England Alliums due to its bright yellow flowers - most of our native and naturalized onions like Wild Garlic, Nodding Onion, and Wild Leek have white, pink, or purplish flowers.

Unlike other wild Alliums in New England like wild garlic or ramps, honey garlic has uniquely drooping, bell-shaped flowers rather than the upright, star-shaped or rounded flower clusters typical of most onion relatives.
